newsitem.title: PERU: Peru police pressure rebels with high-risk tactics.
newsitem.headline: Peru police pressure rebels with high-risk tactics.

text.p: Provocative police tactics aimed at unnerving Marxists holding 72 hostages have heaped pressure on the guerrillas but have also increased fears of bloodshed in the 44-day siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence.

With tactics ranging from the bizarre to the bold, Peru's psychological war against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) has some observers worried that the police could push the rebels too far.

"I'm worried that if the terrorists have been irritated over moves of the special forces ... we are asking for care to be taken about such moves," Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters this week before a planned weekend meeting with Peru's President Alberto Fujimori in Toronto.
In the last week, police have heightened tension by throwing garbage into the residence, blasting martial music and sending a helicopter flying directly overhead.

During a parade of armoured vehicles with police training their guns at the building on Monday, the rebels finally reacted, firing several shots that narrowly missed police who were making obscene gestures at them. Since storming the residence on Dec. 17 and taking hundreds of hostages, the rebels have fired warning shots into the air but this was the first time lives were endangered.

"We understand the need to tighten security at the compound but ask that you give sufficient consideration to preventing accidents or incidents," Japanese spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama quoted Hashimoto as telling Fujimori by phone.

Experts have questioned whether the police tactics would wear down the jungle-trained guerrillas, who have so far showed no sign of weakening resolve. "They are the elite of the MRTA and have the mentality of blind fanatics," psychologist Mariano Querol said.

Monday's gunshots that forced police to withdraw from the area appeared to boost the rebels' morale. "The police came to intimidate and left with their tails between their legs," MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters.
The police manoeuvres were in preparation for a planned assault on the mined and booby-trapped residence, which was the surest way to endanger hostages' lives, Velazco charged.
"The MRTA will not harm its (hostages). The only way they will be killed is by a bullet from the gun of the government's security forces," he added.

With police blasting music at the residence in the early hours, appearing to show more concern about wearing down the rebels than comforting the hostages, commentators reminded the government there were lives at stake.
Cartoonist "Alberto" in the daily La Republica had one character asking what the musical beat from the residence was. "That's the sound of human hearts," his colleague replied.

The Red Cross also complained that police manoeuvres were creating danger. Representatives temporarily stopped humanitarian work until the security forces agreed to respect a "no-go" area while they were at the site.
